title: Source and date
short: Mariana comes from Shakespeare's Measure for Measure, where Angelo has abandoned her at a 'moated grange'. Tennyson first published the poem in Poems, Chiefly Lyrical (1830).
body: In Measure for Measure Mariana is betrothed to Angelo, and he deserts her when her dowry is lost at sea. The Duke mentions that 'at the moated grange resides this dejected Mariana' (3.1). Tennyson's poem, first published in Poems, Chiefly Lyrical (1830) with the epigraph 'Mariana in the moated grange' (not printed in the archive text), takes only that situation and leaves out the play's plot. Tennyson later said that the grange was no particular place but one that grew out of the music of Shakespeare's words. The poem opens on a landscape of decay with no human figure in it. Mariana herself first appears only in the refrain. J. S. Mill (1835) praised Tennyson's power of 'creating scenery, in keeping with some state of human feeling'.

title: peach to the garden-wall
short: This is the early reading. In 1860 Tennyson changed it to 'the pear to the gable-wall', which suits a Lincolnshire farm better.
body: The archive prints the text of 1830–1850s, in which rusted nails fall from the ties that held a peach tree trained against a garden wall. In 1860 Tennyson revised the line to 'the pear to the gable-wall', a hardier fruit and a humbler building. The usual explanation is that this better fits the Lincolnshire fen country he had in mind. Either way the image of decay is exact. The espaliered tree, once kept in order, now sags loose from its supports, an emblem of a life that has lost its frame.

title: moated grange
short: A grange is an outlying farmhouse with its barns, originally one belonging to a religious house. 'Moated' means surrounded by a defensive ditch of water.
body: 'Grange' first meant a granary or barn, then an outlying farm belonging to a monastery, and later any country house with farm buildings. A moat is a deep, wide ditch, usually water-filled, around a house. The phrase comes straight from Measure for Measure (3.1), and for Tennyson's readers it already suggested remoteness and confinement. The moat cuts Mariana off, and its stagnant water returns later as the sluice with 'blacken'd waters' (l. 38). The phrase closes the descriptive section of stanzas 1 and 3 (ll. 8 and 32), just before the refrain.

title: Stanza and refrain
short: Seven twelve-line stanzas of iambic tetrameter rhymed ababcddcefef. Each closes with a four-line refrain that varies only slightly until the last stanza.
body: Each stanza has an eight-line descriptive section (ababcddc) and then a refrain (efef) built on 'dreary' / 'said' / 'aweary' / 'dead'. The tetrameter is short and regular, and the refrain keeps coming back, so time seems to circle without moving forward, which is Mariana's experience. Small changes mark the passage of a day and night ('My life', 'The night', 'The day'). The last stanza breaks the pattern: 'very dreary', 'He will not come', 'She wept', 'Oh God'. The descriptive sections move from garden to house to bed and the house's interior, closing in on her.

title: He cometh not
short: The archaic '-eth' ending gives the refrain a biblical or ballad-like weight. Its simple present tense makes the lover's absence permanent.
body: Mariana's only words in the first six stanzas are the refrain, which never names the absent lover. 'Cometh' is the old third-person form used in the Authorised Version and in ballads, so the plain statement sounds like a lament or a liturgy. The present tense ('cometh not') describes a habitual condition, not a single event. 'Aweary' is an archaic intensive of 'weary' (Macbeth 5.5 has 'I gin to be aweary of the sun'). The wish 'I would that I were dead' turns despair into a formula, repeated until the final stanza's direct cry to God.

anchor: Her tears fell with the dews
title: Tears and dews
short: Her tears are timed to the dew, falling at evening and again before the morning dew has dried, so grief is part of nature's cycle.
body: The parallel 'Her tears fell with the dews at even; / Her tears fell ere the dews were dried' makes weeping as regular and impersonal as dew. Grief takes up the whole day. She cannot bear to look at 'the sweet heaven, / Either at morn or eventide'. The pathetic fallacy in this poem goes both ways. The landscape reflects her feeling and her feeling becomes a natural process. Mill singled the poem out for the way scenery carries emotion.

title: trance the sky
short: A disputed verb. Editors gloss it as 'cross, traverse' or as 'cast a spell on, hold unnaturally still'.
body: 'When thickest dark did trance the sky' uses 'trance' as a transitive verb, which is rare. One line of editors (E. K. Brown) takes it as a form of 'transe' or 'traverse', meaning darkness passes across the sky. Others (Beck and Snow) read it as 'entrance', meaning darkness holds the sky still as if under a spell. The second reading fits the poem's atmosphere of suspended time and Mariana's own half-dreaming state ('In sleep she seem'd to walk forlorn', l. 30). Ricks records the difficulty.

title: glooming flats
short: 'Athwart' means across. The 'glooming flats' are the darkening, level fenland of Tennyson's native Lincolnshire.
body: 'Athwart' is a literary form meaning across, from side to side. 'Glooming' means growing dark and is a favourite Tennysonian participle. The 'flats' are low-lying level land such as fen and marsh. Tennyson grew up at Somersby in Lincolnshire, and the poem's level waste, fen, sluices and lone poplar are often traced to that landscape. It contrasts with the Italianate setting of the later 'Mariana in the South' (1832). Her glance across the flats is a look of waiting, but nothing comes over the horizon.

title: night-fowl, cock
short: The night-bird and the cock crowing an hour before light mark the empty hours. In folklore the cock's crow signals the end of night spirits.
body: This stanza opens at midnight ('Upon the middle of the night'; the full stop after it is in the archive text) and moves through sounds Mariana hears in the dark: a crowing 'night-fowl', the cock singing 'an hour ere light', oxen lowing from the fen. 'Night-fowl' may mean a nocturnal bird, or the cock itself heard crowing in the dead of night. The cock's crow before dawn traditionally drives away ghosts, as in Hamlet 1.1. The 'old faces' of l. 66 later come back to haunt her all the same.

title: gray-eyed morn
short: This echoes Friar Laurence's 'The grey-eyed morn smiles on the frowning night' in Romeo and Juliet.
body: Romeo and Juliet 2.3 opens with Friar Laurence's 'The grey-eyed morn smiles on the frowning night'. Tennyson borrows the epithet, but the effect is cold. His morning is woken by 'cold winds' and brings only another dreary day. The Shakespearean echo suits a poem that is grown from a Shakespearean phrase. Here 'gray' (Tennyson's spelling) means pale, colourless dawn light.

anchor: A sluice with blacken'd waters slept
title: Sluice
short: A sluice is a channel or gate controlling water. Here its black water lies motionless, an image of stagnation.
body: A sluice is an artificial channel for water fitted with a gate, common in drained fen country. 'About a stone-cast from the wall' (a stone's throw) it lies 'blacken'd' and asleep, and the verb 'slept' carries over to the landscape the torpor that Mariana suffers. The blackness picks up the 'blackest moss' of l. 1. Water that ought to flow is held back, as her life is.

title: marish
short: 'Marish' is an archaic and poetic form of 'marsh'.
body: 'Marish' (from Old French mareis) was by 1830 a poetic archaism for marsh. It gives the line a Spenserian, antique colour. The 'cluster'd' mosses, 'many, round and small', that 'crept' over the sluice continue the poem's imagery of slow overgrowth. Everything in Mariana's world moves only by creeping, crusting or decaying. The word belongs to the poem's fenland vocabulary, along with 'sluice', 'flats' and 'fen', and like them it fixes the setting in real, drained marsh country.

anchor: Hard by a poplar shook alway
title: The poplar
short: The single poplar, the only tree 'for leagues', is the poem's most discussed image. It stands for the absent lover, for time, or simply for loneliness.
body: 'Hard by' means close by, and 'alway' is an archaic form of 'always'. The poplar, 'silver-green with gnarled bark', is the only vertical feature in the 'level waste'. It returns twice. Its shadow falls 'Upon her bed, across her brow' (ll. 55–56), and its sound in the wind helps 'confound / Her sense' (ll. 76–77). Critics have read it in several ways: as a substitute for the absent male presence (some see a sexual threat in the shadow on the bed), as a figure of unceasing restless motion beside her stillness, or as a plain realist detail of fen country. The poem does not decide between them.

anchor: wild winds bound within their cell
title: Winds bound in their cell
short: When the winds are shut up 'within their cell', the image may recall Aeolus keeping the winds in a cave in Virgil, and the poplar's shadow falls still across her bed.
body: In Aeneid 1.52–63 Aeolus, king of the winds, holds the struggling winds in a vast cave and keeps them in chains and prison. Tennyson's phrase 'bound within their cell' may recall that classical picture. When the winds are free ('up and away') the shadow sways in the white curtain. When they are imprisoned and the moon is low, the shadow lies across Mariana. The movement from 'gusty shadow' to a shadow that falls 'Upon her bed, across her brow' is the poem's closest approach to bodily contact. For that reason critics read it as a ghostly stand-in for the absent lover, or a premonition of death.

title: Blue fly, mouse
short: A bluebottle buzzing at the window and a mouse shrieking behind the rotting panelling are minute details of a house given over to decay.
body: The 'blue fly' is the bluebottle, a fly associated with rotting matter, and 'sung i' the pane' gives its buzzing against the glass a mock-musical sound. The mouse 'Behind the mouldering wainscot' (a wainscot is wooden panelling lining the lower walls of a room) shrieks and peers from the crevice. These close-up details made the poem famous for its 'Pre-Raphaelite' precision before the movement existed. Millais's painting Mariana (1851), exhibited with lines from the poem, draws on this world of detail. Mill praised the poem's 'vivid feeling of physical and spiritual dreariness'.

anchor: Old faces glimmer'd thro' the doors
title: Old faces, footsteps, voices
short: Mariana's isolation begins to produce hallucinations, ghosts of the past seen and heard about the house.
body: The repeated 'Old faces ... Old footsteps ... Old voices' is anaphora, and it fills the empty house with presences. They may be memories, ghosts of earlier inhabitants, or the effects of solitude on the mind. 'Glimmer'd' leaves it unclear whether anything is seen at all. This is the poem's psychological climax before the last stanza. The 'dreamy house' (l. 61) has become an image of her own mind.

title: Thick-moted sunbeam
short: Most of all she hates late afternoon, when a sunbeam full of floating dust lies across the rooms and the day sinks west.
body: Motes are specks of dust made visible in a beam of light. The 'thick-moted sunbeam' slanting 'Athwart the chambers' is beautiful in itself, but to Mariana it shows how much time has passed and how much dust has gathered. The day is personified, 'sloping toward his western bower', the sun going to rest in its bower (a lady's chamber or a shady retreat), a pastoral and mythic touch. She 'loath'd' this hour above all, because the evening ends another day of waiting and begins the night.

title: The final refrain
short: The last refrain changes: 'very dreary', 'He will not come', 'She wept', 'Oh God'. Habit becomes certainty and despair turns to prayer.
body: For the first time the refrain changes its key words. 'He cometh not' (habitual present) becomes 'He will not come' (a future certainty). 'She said' becomes 'She wept'. 'I would that I were dead' becomes 'Oh God, that I were dead'. The poem does not end with an event, only with a recognition. Readers who know Measure for Measure know that the deserted Mariana will in fact be married to Angelo in the end, but Tennyson cuts off any rescue. Critics have found here an early statement of Tennyson's poetry of paralysed waiting (compare 'The Lady of Shalott', 1832).
